subject: gravity at the poles
title: What If You Weighed Yourself at the North Pole?

scenes.text: What if you weighed yourself at the North Pole? Same body, same scale. A different number.
At the poles, gravity pulls at about 9.83 metres per second squared. At the equator, only about 9.78.
That's about half a percent. A 150-pound person would weigh almost a pound more at the pole.
Reason one: Earth spins. At the equator you're moving at about 1,000 miles an hour, flung slightly outward.
Reason two: that spin makes Earth bulge. The equator sits about 13 miles farther from the centre than the poles.
And the lightest spot on the planet isn't a beach on the equator. It's the summit of Huascaran, a mountain in Peru.

description:
What if you weighed yourself at the North Pole? Surface gravity is about 9.83 m/s squared at the poles and 9.78 at the equator, a difference of about half a percent.
Earth's spin flings you outward at the equator and makes the planet bulge about 21 km (13 miles) wider there, and the weakest gravity on Earth's surface is on the summit of Huascaran in Peru.
